emerging_technology: AI-enabled general-purpose humanoid robots controlled by learned robot foundation models (vision-language-action, VLA), e.g. Agility Digit, Figure, Boston Dynamics Atlas, Apptronik Apollo, with model layers such as Gemini Robotics and NVIDIA Isaac GR00T
intended_application: Moving plastic totes between autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), conveyors and racks at tote-transfer stations in e-commerce fulfillment warehouses; picking of individual items, truck loading and any work in public areas are out of scope.
organization: Hypothetical mid-size U.S. third-party logistics (3PL) provider: six fulfillment warehouses in the Southeast, about 1,400 employees, contract fulfillment for retail and consumer-goods clients under service-level agreements. Two sites already run conveyors and about 60 AMRs; tote transfer between AMRs and conveyors is done by associates on two shifts.
industry_sector: Third-party logistics and warehousing (contract e-commerce fulfillment)
business_need: Reduce hard-to-staff, repetitive and ergonomically risky tote-transfer work (high turnover and recurring strain reports at transfer stations) without missing client service levels; no measured productivity, cost or safety benefit from humanoids is assumed.
users_stakeholders: DECISION OWNER: VP Operations (business-unit leader in the team's Lab 1 decision map); the CFO approves any capital or multi-year contract. Also: site general managers, the environment-health-and-safety (EHS) manager, maintenance technicians, warehouse associates at transfer stations, client account managers, and clients whose service levels depend on throughput.
adoption_posture: Pragmatic fast follower: adopts automation after peers show repeatable results; will run small, reversible trials, but requires EHS sign-off before any robot works near people and will not commit multi-year capital without measured results.
capabilities_constraints: ORG READINESS FACTS (hypothetical): 1 STAGE ASKED AND SCOPE: possible bounded evaluation at one transfer station at one site for about 12 weeks; no decision on scope beyond that. 2 SPONSOR: the VP Operations sponsors any evaluation and can stop it. 3 COORDINATOR / OPERATING OWNER: Not stated. 4 APPROVED ENVIRONMENT: one AMR-to-conveyor station that could be fenced or zoned away from foot traffic; no public access; no data or video-retention permission decided. 5 CONTRACTS: no vendor contract, robots-as-a-service agreement or client consent covering robots at client-dedicated stations. 6 BUDGET / PROTECTED HOURS: no evaluation budget approved; protected staff hours Not stated. 7 REVIEW / FALLBACK: manual tote transfer stays available; a stop-and-fallback procedure has not been written or demonstrated. 8 GOVERNANCE REVIEWS: EHS has not reviewed humanoid robots; client contracts not reviewed. 9 SKILLS: maintenance technicians service the existing AMRs and conveyors; no humanoid or robot-learning experience; training owner Not stated. 10 OBJECTIONS: associates raised job-displacement concerns at a site meeting; no unsanctioned use. Other: the warehouse management system integrates with the AMR fleet; IT can provide network access in a fenced zone.
risk_consequence_context: Physical-safety risk to associates working near dynamically balancing robots; dropped or damaged client goods; throughput loss and service-level penalties if a station stalls; capital or multi-year robots-as-a-service commitments that are costly to exit; labor-relations and reputational effects. A fenced single-station evaluation with manual fallback is reversible; a multi-site contract is not.
management_question: Should this 3PL adopt, run a bounded experiment, run a proof of concept, monitor, defer, or reject AI-enabled humanoid robots for tote transfer between AMRs and conveyors now? What would have to be true before it commits capital or a multi-year contract, can the organization support the stage it would start with, and what should it watch?
time_horizon: 12 months; FY2027 capital plan is set in Q1 2027. No deployment date is implied.
additional_context:
ASSESSMENT DATE: 2026-11-24. All organizational details are hypothetical exercise assumptions, not facts about a real company. ## S1 Google DeepMind: Gemini Robotics 2 brings whole-body intelligence to robots
- URL: https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-robotics-2-brings-whole-body-intelligence-to-robots/
- Date: 2026-07-30; Accessed: 2026-11-24
- Source class: vendor-claim
- Supports: DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2, a vision-language-action (VLA) model for full humanoids and bi-arm robots, together with Gemini Robotics ER 2 (an embodied-reasoning planner; available in Google AI Studio) and On-Device 2. The VLA and On-Device models are for early-access partners only. In DeepMind's own tests, whole-body manipulation on Apptronik Apollo succeeded 68.4% of the time picking from a table, 45.7% from the floor and 76.3% from a shelf. The page says dexterous manipulation remains hard. Named partners: Apptronik, Boston Dynamics, Agile Robots.
- Limits / forbidden inference: Vendor-run tests. The page does not mention warehouses, totes or logistics. The models are early access, not generally available, and no customer deployment is shown. Being named a partner does not show the model is in use in any operation.

## S9 Chen et al. (preprint, arXiv:2607.04434): RoboDojo: A Unified Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Generalist Robot Manipulation Policies
- URL: https://huggingface.co/papers/2607.04434
- Date: 2026-07-05 (v1; v3 2026-07-08); Accessed: 2026-11-24
- Source class: independent (non-peer-reviewed preprint)
- Supports: Ten generalist VLA policies were evaluated on 18 real-world tasks across three bimanual arm platforms. The best (pi0.5) reached 12.8% overall success; GR00T-N1.7 reached 1.7%; human teleoperation reached 100%. In simulation (42 tasks) the best policy averaged 8.80%, against 76.03% for human experts.
- Limits / forbidden inference: Tabletop bimanual arms, not humanoids, and not tote handling. Gemini Robotics 2 and GR00T 2 were not evaluated. A preprint, read in part. The tasks are deliberately diverse and hard, so these are not failure rates for narrow, engineered warehouse deployments.
